Mm-hmm. Yeah, I think we will see more and more of that. And to me, this is very consistent with what we were discussing about data, right? You want the model to be good at coding, you give it coding problems, let it try, and give it feedback on whether the solution works. For some other tasks, getting reliable feedback is much harder. And for a general model, we still have this coverage problem: how do we provide enough diversity of experiences for all the things we want it to do? I think building those environments will be a big part of the work. Yeah.

sol.text:
Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm. Yeah, I think we will see more and more of these environments, especially for tasks where the outcome can be verified automatically, like coding, mathematics, or using a computer. In that case, reinforcement learning gives the model not only examples of successful solutions, but also the opportunity to try, fail, and receive a very clear signal about what worked. So it is a very powerful way of generating additional training data.

But I don't think the environment itself solves everything. The model will learn what the environment and the reward function teach it, right? If the environment covers only a narrow set of tasks, or if the reward is imperfect, the model may become very good at exploiting that particular setup without becoming generally more capable. In some sense, we have moved the data-curation problem into an environment-curation problem: what tasks do we include, how diverse are they, and does success inside the environment correspond to what users actually want?

And for many important abilities, the reward is not easy to define. Coding has tests; mathematics can sometimes have a verifier. But for writing, counseling, or visual understanding, there may not be one objective score. So I think reinforcement learning and environments will be a very important part of the future, but mainly where we can build rich, diverse, and reliable feedback. Pretraining on broad data will still provide the general capability, and reinforcement learning will help the model practice and improve on particular abilities. Yeah.

Yeah. Mm-hmm. I think, I think it's, it's a very natural continuation of what we just discussed, actually. So, if you, if you think about it, building an environment is just another way of, of collecting data, right? It's, it's data that you don't have to, to curate from the internet, you, you generate it yourself with the model, and, and the environment gives you the, the supervision signal, the reward. So in that sense, I, I don't see it as a, as a fundamentally different paradigm from, from what people have been doing with, with data curation. It's the same lesson. If you want the model to be good at coding, you, you build a coding environment, you, you train on that. If you want it to be good at, at using a browser, you build that environment. it's, it's just, "if you want the model to be good at something, you better train it on that something," but, but in a different form. Yeah.

but I, I do think there are, there are two things that, that concern me a little bit. one is that, the domains where this works really well right now are the ones where, where verification is easy, right? Code, math, these, these have clear, automatic, checkable answers. And a lot of the things that, that people actually use these models for in daily life are, are not like that. like, how do you build an environment for, for writing a good email or, or for, for the psychological counseling example I, I mentioned earlier? So, so I think there, we, we still rely a lot on, on human preference, on, on reward models, and, and those are, are much noisier and much easier to, to game. so I, I'm, I'm a little worried that the field, we, we optimize on what's, what's measurable rather than what, what actually matters, just because, the environment is there.

and the second thing is, does it transfer? like, if you train on a thousand environments, do you get a model that's good on the thousand-and-first one it has never seen? and this is, this is really the same question as, as the dataset bias work, right? we, we found that, that these large scale datasets, they are still very different from each other, they, they don't cover, the, the whole space. And, and I would guess environments are, are much worse in that regard, because each one is, is hand-designed by, by some team with, with some specific task in mind. So the, the coverage problem is, is going to be even more severe. so, so I, I would love to see, more studies on, on held-out environments, like, like people just, just don't train on a whole family of tasks and, and see what happens. that, that's the experiment I would want to see.

and, and also, I think a lot of what RL is doing right now is, is eliciting rather than, than teaching, right? the, the capability mostly has to be there in the, in the base model already, from pre-training, and, and RL kind of sharpens it, makes the model, use it reliably. so, so again it comes back to, to the pre-training data. if, if it's not in there, I, I don't think the environment can, can put it in from scratch, at least not efficiently. So, so yes, I do think we'll see more and more environments, it's, it's clearly where a lot of the, the effort is going. but I, I wouldn't say it replaces the data question. It's, it's the data question wearing, wearing a different hat. Yeah.

Yeah. I, I think this is very much the same story as, as what I was saying earlier, right? If you want the model to be good at something, you, you better train it on that something. And these environments are, are basically a way to, to generate that training signal, that feedback, in a, in a much more targeted way than, than just next-token prediction on internet text.

So, so coding is a, is a good example. You can read a lot of GitHub, and that helps, but if the model can actually try, try a patch, run the tests, get a pass or fail, that’s a much cleaner signal than, than just imitating whatever is in the training set. Same for, for other verifiable tasks. So I do think we will see more and more of this. I, I don’t think that’s a coincidence that labs are building their own environments. It’s, it’s the natural next step once you, you kind of accept that the model only learns what you, you actually put in front of it.

But I, I wouldn’t say that’s the whole future, or that we just, just keep stacking environments and that’s it. Because an environment is still data, in a, in a way. It’s a, a very curated form of data, of training signal. And the same lessons apply. If your environment only covers one style of problems, the model will be good at that style and maybe not at the rest. It’s, it’s a bit like the dataset bias thing we talked about. These environments can look diverse from the outside, and the model can still pick up very specific cues about what you actually rewarded.

And then there’s this trade-off I mentioned. If you spend a lot of compute RL-ing on one environment, you are specializing the model. That’s, that’s fine if that’s the product you want, a coding model, a, a math model. For a general assistant, you still need coverage. You cannot only have a coding environment and expect everything else to stay good. Capabilities still compete a bit under limited compute.

So, so I, I see RL and these environments as, as another way of doing the data mixture, just with a, a closed loop and a score instead of a static dataset. The architecture of the RL algorithm, I, I would tend to think that matters less than, than what the environment actually asks for, and how diverse and how well-specified that reward is. That’s, that’s the part I would watch. Yeah.

gemini.text:
Yeah. I think, yeah, this is definitely a very promising and exciting direction, especially recently with the rise of these reasoning models, right? 

I think the reason reinforcement learning works so well in domains like coding or math is because you have a clear verifier. You have unit tests, you have compilers, you have ground-truth answers where the reward signal is objective and clean. And this connects back to what we were just talking about: if you want the model to be good at reasoning through a problem, trying out different steps, and correcting itself, you really need to put it in an environment where it can explore, make mistakes, and get feedback on whether the final outcome is correct. Pre-training on internet text alone just gives you imitation of human text, but RL lets the model search and optimize beyond human demonstrations.

So I do think for verifiable domains, this is absolutely where a lot of progress is happening, and we will definitely see more and more specialized environments and synthetic pipelines being built. 

The main challenge, though, is how do you scale this outside of math and coding? In the real world, for most open-ended tasks—like creative writing, or general dialogue, or complex multimodal planning—it's very hard to write an automated verifier. Reward modeling is noisy, and models are very good at finding shortcuts or hacking the reward. So in a way, the bottleneck shifts from curating static data to designing good environments and reliable reward signals. But yeah, for domains where we can define clear rules and feedback, I think RL and environment-based training is definitely the right way to go.

Mm-hmm. Yeah, I, I think it's very consistent with what I, I just said, right? If you want the model to be good at something, you need to train it on that something. And, and reinforcement learning with environments is, to me, is just another way of, of getting training data. It's, it's a data collection mechanism. So, so instead of collecting a static dataset from the internet, you, you build an environment and the model generates its own data by, by interacting with it, and the environment gives you the, the signal, the reward. So I, I would still frame it as a data problem, not, not really a, a fundamentally new thing. The, the interface is different, but the, the lesson is the same.

And, and I do think we will see more and more of this, because for a lot of tasks we care about, coding, math, using, using tools, the, the internet just doesn't have, the data doesn't exist naturally, right? Nobody writes down like every step of, of how they debug a program with the, the feedback from the compiler. So you have to, you have to create that. And, and for these tasks, it's very natural because the reward is, is verifiable. You can run the code, you can check the answer. that's, that's why coding and math came first, I think. It's not a coincidence.

But, but the, the hard part is, is when you go beyond that. So, like what I said before about the data mixture, you, you now have the same problem with environments. How many environments do you need? How do you balance them? if you train on, on a thousand coding environments, does the model become good at, at the, the coding environment, or, or good at coding, right? These are, these are not the same thing. It's, it's the same dataset bias story. The model can, can pick up cues from the, the environment that, that don't transfer to what the real user is, is actually doing. And, and also for a lot of things, like writing, or, or like helping someone with, with a personal problem, it's very hard to define a, a reward that's, that's not, that doesn't get, gamed by the model.

So I, I, yeah, I think it's the future in the sense that this is how, how the labs will get data on tasks that, that don't have natural data. but, but I don't think it replaces the, the pre-training data story. It's, it's on top of it. And, and from an academic point of view, it's, it's a little bit, sad, because building good environments is, is very engineering heavy, and, and, we, we cannot really afford to build, hundreds of them. So, so what we can do maybe is, is study the generalization question. Like, does, does training on one environment transfer to another, and, and why or why not. I think that's, that's still a very open question that, that doesn't need frontier scale to, to study. Yeah.
